headline: Nu Holdings: revenue up 39% and profit up 39% to $1.09 billion, as Mexico becomes a full bank; credit costs rise 71%
takeaway: Revenue rose 39% to $5.8 billion and net income 39% to $1.09 billion, or $0.22 a share, in line with forecasts. Provisions for credit losses grew faster, up 71%, but a lower tax rate and strong fee growth carried the quarter, and the shares rose 7%.
results: Nu Holdings reported total revenue of $5,820 million for the third quarter, up 39% from $4,173 million a year earlier. Interest income and gains rose 40% to $5,003 million and fee and commission income rose 37% to $817 million. Interest and funding expenses rose only 23%, so the spread between what Nu earns on credit and pays on deposits widened.

Expected credit losses — the provisions Nu sets aside for bad loans — rose 71% to $1,668 million, faster than revenue, and gross profit rose 34% to $2,437 million. Operating expenses rose 55%, with general and administrative costs up 69% and marketing up 79%. Pre-tax income rose 21% to $1,350 million, but the effective tax rate fell to 19% from 30%, lifting net income 39% to $1,092 million.

Diluted EPS was $0.2235 against $0.1595 a year earlier and a consensus of $0.2228. Over nine months net income rose 53% to $3.0 billion. Total assets reached $87.4 billion, up from $74.9 billion at the end of 2025, including $22.4 billion of credit card receivables and $12.2 billion of other loans.
mgmt: The quarterly financial statements highlight a regulatory milestone: Nu’s Mexican subsidiary received authorisation from the national banking regulator in July to operate as a full multiple-service bank and began operating as Nubank Mexico on August 6, 2026. The company said it aims to expand its credit and financial products in Mexico, where it has so far grown mainly through credit cards and high-yield deposit accounts.
Nu also continued to build its operations in Colombia, and the rise in general, administrative and marketing costs reflects the investment in those two markets alongside its core Brazilian business.
view: Nu is the most successful digital bank built anywhere in the past decade, and this quarter shows a business still compounding profit at close to 40% a year. The economics are simple: an app-only bank in Brazil, where incumbents charged some of the highest fees in the world, can acquire customers for a few dollars, serve them for under a dollar a month and lend to them at rates of 50% or more. The challenge is that this model only works if the credit book stays clean, and the 71% rise in provisions is the number to watch.

Provisions growing faster than revenue are not automatically a warning. Under IFRS 9, a bank must provision upfront for expected losses on new loans, so a lender growing its book quickly — and moving into longer, larger personal and secured loans — will show rising provisions before the interest income on those loans arrives. Nu’s widening funding spread suggests the new lending is profitable. But Brazilian household debt is high and interest rates there remain elevated, so a turn in the credit cycle would hit Nu harder than a traditional bank with a more diversified, lower-yield book.

The cost line deserves attention too. Expenses up 55% against revenue up 39% reflects the Mexican bank launch and the Colombian build-out, and in a strict sense the quarter’s profit growth depended on a lower tax rate. At around 14 times trailing earnings the shares are not expensive for that growth, but much of the upside rests on Mexico becoming a second Brazil. The licence is the necessary first step; the evidence will come from Mexican deposit and lending growth over the next few quarters.
watch: Watch the ratio of credit-loss provisions to revenue and Brazilian delinquency trends, deposit and loan growth at the new Nubank Mexico, and whether the lower tax rate is sustainable.
